unit-alg-t4-03.title: Topic 4 · 4-3 Multiplying and Dividing Rational Expressions
unit-alg-t4-03.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 4-3: Multiplying and Dividing Rational Expressions

summary.text: Lesson 4-3 simplifies, multiplies and divides rational expressions: factoring and dividing out common factors, opposite factors that leave −1, writing equivalent expressions over a stated domain, multiplying by a polynomial, dividing by multiplying by the reciprocal, and simplifying ratios such as surface area to volume.

why.text: Every later rational skill — adding, solving equations, graphing — starts with factoring and cancelling correctly. The domain restriction that travels with each answer is what makes the algebra honest about the holes in the graph.

objectives.text: Simplify a rational expression and state the values excluded from its domain
Multiply rational expressions, including by a polynomial
Divide rational expressions by multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor
Explain why only common factors, never terms, can be divided out

parentNote.text: The single most common error is cancelling TERMS instead of factors — crossing out the x² in (x² + 6x)/(x² + 3x) — and several questions are built to catch it, along with a one-number check that exposes it. The second is the domain: restrictions come from the ORIGINAL denominators, and when dividing, from the divisor's numerator as well. Many answers here are marked wrong in class for a missing restriction rather than a wrong expression.

nextUp.text: Start with the "factors, not terms" cards — every question here depends on them.

cards.def:
**A rational expression is simplified when its numerator and denominator share no common factor other than 1.**
• (x + 6)/(x + 3) is simplified; x(x + 6)/(x(x + 3)) is not.
• Simplifying never changes the values — only the domain statement has to travel with it.
cards.hint: No shared FACTOR left, top and bottom.

cards.def:
**Factor the numerator and the denominator completely, then divide out the factors they share.**
• (x² − 25)/(x² + 2x − 15) = (x − 5)(x + 5)/((x + 5)(x − 3)) = (x − 5)/(x − 3).
• If you cannot see a common factor, you have not finished factoring.
cards.hint: Factor everything before you cancel anything.

cards.def:
**Only a factor of the WHOLE numerator and the WHOLE denominator can be divided out.**
• (x + 6)/x is not 6: the x on top is a term added to 6, not a factor of the top.
• Test it: at x = 2, (2 + 6)/2 = 4, not 6.
cards.hint: If it is joined by + or −, it is a term — hands off.

cards.def:
**a − b and b − a are opposites, so (a − b)/(b − a) = −1.**
• 4 − x = −(x − 4), so (4 − x)/(x − 4) simplifies to −1, not 1.
• Pull out the −1 first, then cancel.
cards.hint: Same numbers, reversed order: that is a factor of −1.

cards.term: The domain travels with the answer
cards.def:
**Values that made ANY original denominator zero stay excluded, even after their factor has cancelled.**
• (x² − 25)/(x² + 2x − 15) equals (x − 5)/(x − 3) only for x ≠ −5 and x ≠ 3.
• An identity between two expressions holds only where both are defined.
cards.hint: Read the restrictions off the ORIGINAL, before cancelling.

cards.def:
**Multiply top and bottom by the same nonzero expression — a form of 1 — and add its zeros to the domain restrictions.**
• (x + 1)/(x − 4) · (x + 2)/(x + 2) = (x² + 3x + 2)/(x² − 2x − 8), for x ≠ 4, −2.
• The new expression agrees with the old one everywhere both are defined.
cards.hint: A form of 1 changes the look, never the value.

cards.def:
**Factor every numerator and denominator, multiply straight across, and divide out the common factors.**
• Cancelling before you multiply out saves a lot of work.
• State the domain from every denominator that appeared.
cards.hint: Factor, then cancel, then multiply — in that order.

cards.def:
**Write the polynomial over 1, then multiply as usual.**
• (x + 3)/(x² − 25) · (x² − 5x) = (x + 3)/((x − 5)(x + 5)) · x(x − 5)/1 = x(x + 3)/(x + 5).
• Restrictions: x ≠ 5 and x ≠ −5.

**Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor, then simplify as for multiplication.**
• A/B ÷ C/D = A/B · D/C.
• The divisor's NUMERATOR moves to the bottom, so its zeros join the restrictions too.
cards.hint: Keep, change, flip — then watch the new denominator.

cards.def:
**For A/B ÷ C/D, exclude the zeros of B, of D, AND of C.**
• B and D are denominators from the start.
• C becomes a denominator once you flip the divisor — and you cannot divide by zero anyway.
cards.hint: Three places to look, not two.

cards.def:
**A fraction whose numerator or denominator contains a fraction is a division problem in disguise.**
• (A/B) over (C/D) means A/B ÷ C/D.
• Rewrite it as a division, then multiply by the reciprocal.
cards.hint: The long fraction bar is a ÷ sign.

cards.def:
**Multiply coefficients, then combine powers of each variable by subtracting exponents across the fraction bar.**
• (4x³y)/(6xy²) = 2x²/(3y), for x ≠ 0, y ≠ 0.
• Every variable that ever sat in a denominator is restricted from being 0.
cards.hint: Numbers with numbers, x with x, y with y.

cards.term: Ratio of surface area to volume
cards.def:
**SA/V compares packaging used to space held; for similar shapes it simplifies to a number over the length, so the shape with the smaller number is more efficient for every size.**
• A cube of edge 2x: SA = 24x², V = 8x³, so SA/V = 3/x.
• Simplifying the ratio is just dividing rational expressions.
cards.hint: Smaller SA/V: less wrapping per unit of space.

questions.q: When is a rational expression in simplified form?
opts: When its numerator and denominator share no common factor other than 1
When no variable appears anywhere in its denominator at all
When the degree of its numerator is less than its denominator's
When every term appearing on both top and bottom has been crossed out
questions.hint: Simplifying is about factors.
steps: Simplifying means dividing out common factors.
You stop when there are none left except 1.
Variables in the denominator are fine, and degrees can be anything.
Simplified form: no common factor other than 1.

ex.main: **When the numerator and denominator share no common factor other than 1.** Crossing out matching TERMS is the classic mistake, and it changes the value. A simplified expression can easily have a variable underneath or a top-heavy degree.
ex.tip: Factors, not terms. Always.

questions.q: Simplify (x² − 49)/(x² + 4x − 21).
questions.hint: Factor top and bottom, then look for the shared factor.
steps: Divide out the common factor x + 7.

ex.main: **(x − 7)/(x − 3).** The factor x + 7 is shared, so it divides out, leaving the other two. (x + 7)/(x − 3) keeps the factor that cancelled; 7/3 cancels the x² terms as if they were factors.
ex.tip: Factored form makes the shared factor impossible to miss.

questions.q: Which values of x must be excluded from (x + 2)/(x² − 9x)?
questions.hint: Exclusions come from the denominator only.
steps: It is zero when x = 0 or x = 9.
The numerator's zero, x = −2, just makes the expression 0, which is allowed.

ex.main: **0 and 9.** x(x − 9) = 0 at both. Forgetting the factor x gives "9 only", and −2 makes the whole expression 0 — a perfectly good value.
ex.tip: Factor the denominator fully; a common factor of x is easy to miss.

questions.q: Simplify (5 − x)/(x − 5), for x ≠ 5.
questions.hint: Write 5 − x as −1 times something.
steps: The x − 5 divides out, leaving the −1.

ex.main: **−1.** The top and bottom are opposites, not equals. Try x = 7: (5 − 7)/(7 − 5) = −2/2 = −1. Answering 1 misses the sign that reversing the subtraction brings in.
ex.tip: Reversed subtraction hides a factor of −1.

questions.q: What is the first move when you divide one rational expression by another?
opts: Multiply the first by the reciprocal of the second
Divide the numerators, then divide the denominators
Cross-multiply so that both fraction bars disappear
Flip the first expression, then multiply by the second
questions.hint: It works exactly like dividing ordinary fractions.
steps: A/B ÷ C/D is the same as A/B · D/C.
The first expression stays as it is.
Only the divisor — the second expression — is flipped.

ex.main: **Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor.** It is the fraction rule you already know. Flipping the FIRST expression instead gives the reciprocal of the right answer, and cross-multiplying is for solving equations, not simplifying.
ex.tip: Keep the first, flip the second.

questions.q: Simplify (6x²y)/(5z) · (10z²)/(3xy³).
questions.hint: Numbers with numbers, then each variable on its own.
steps: x: x²/x = x.   z: z²/z = z.

ex.main: **4xz/y².** Each variable is handled on its own: two x's on top against one below leaves x; one y on top against three below leaves y² underneath. 4xz/y cancels only one y; 4x²z/y² forgets the x in the second denominator.
ex.tip: Count each variable top and bottom, then subtract.

questions.q: Why is (x + 6)/x NOT equal to 6?
opts: It does not equal 6 only when x is 0; everywhere else it does
It does equal 6, because the two x's divide out to leave just 6
x is a term of the top, not a factor of it, so it cannot cancel
Because the numerator has degree 1 and the denominator does too
questions.hint: Try a value: x = 2.
steps: The top is x + 6, a SUM; x is one of its terms.
Only a factor of the whole numerator can be divided out.

ex.main: **Because x is a term of the numerator, not a factor.** A single number check settles it: x = 2 gives 4. The expression can be split as x/x + 6/x = 1 + 6/x, which shows exactly what cancelling really allows.
ex.tip: If one number breaks a "simplification", it was never true.

questions.q: Multiply and simplify: (x² − 4)/(x + 5) · (x² + 8x + 15)/(x² + x − 6). State the domain.
opts: x + 2, for every real number x
questions.hint: Factor all four polynomials; collect restrictions from both denominators BEFORE cancelling.
steps: Cancel x + 5, x + 3 and x − 2: the product is x + 2, for x ≠ −5, −3, 2.

ex.main: **x + 2, for x ≠ −5, −3, 2.** Every factor except x + 2 cancels, but each one that came from a denominator leaves its restriction behind. "Every real number" is the graph of y = x + 2 with no holes, which is not this expression.
ex.tip: Write the restrictions down before you cross anything out.

questions.q: Divide and simplify: (x² − 16)/(3x) ÷ (x + 4)/(6x²).
questions.hint: Multiply by the reciprocal of (x + 4)/(6x²).

ex.main: **2x(x − 4).** After flipping, x + 4 and 3x both cancel. (x − 4)/(2x) flips the wrong expression, and (x − 4)(x + 4)²/(18x³) is what you get by multiplying without flipping at all.
ex.tip: Flip the divisor, then it is an ordinary product.

questions.q: What is the domain of (x + 1)/(x − 2) ÷ (x − 3)/(x + 5)?
questions.hint: Check both original denominators — and the divisor's numerator.
steps: The original denominators are x − 2 and x + 5, so x ≠ 2 and x ≠ −5.
Now x − 3 is a denominator too, so x ≠ 3 — and at x = 3 you would be dividing by 0.

ex.main: **x ≠ 2, −5 and 3.** The trap is the divisor's numerator: when the divisor is 0 the whole division is undefined, and flipping it puts x − 3 underneath. −1 only makes the first fraction 0, which is allowed.
ex.tip: Dividing: three places to look for restrictions, not two.

questions.q: Multiply and simplify: (x + 3)/(x² − 25) · (x² − 5x).
questions.hint: Write x² − 5x over 1 and factor everything.

ex.main: **x(x + 3)/(x + 5).** The x − 5 cancels but the x stays. (x + 3)/(x + 5) loses that x, x(x + 3)/(x − 5) cancels the wrong factor, and putting x² − 5x underneath treats the multiplication as a division.
ex.tip: A polynomial multiplies the TOP; write it over 1 so it lands there.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to (x + 1)/(x − 4) over the domain x ≠ 4, −2?
questions.hint: Which form of 1 brings in the restriction x ≠ −2?
steps: To exclude x = −2, multiply top and bottom by (x + 2)/(x + 2).

ex.main: **(x² + 3x + 2)/(x² − 2x − 8).** (x² + x)/(x² − 4x) also has the same values, but it was made with x/x, so its domain is x ≠ 4, 0 — the wrong domain. Adding 2 to top and bottom, as in (x + 3)/(x − 2), changes the value completely.
ex.tip: Equivalent expressions are only equivalent on a stated domain.

questions.q: Simplify (x³ − 4x)/(x² + 4x + 4).
questions.hint: Factor out x first on top, then spot the perfect square underneath.
steps: One factor of x + 2 divides out; one stays underneath.

ex.main: **x(x − 2)/(x + 2).** The bottom is (x + 2) TWICE, so only one copy cancels. x(x − 2) cancels both; (x − 2)/(x + 2) drops the common factor x that was pulled out first.
ex.tip: A squared factor cancels once per matching factor, no more.

questions.q: Simplify the complex fraction whose numerator is (x + 1)/x and whose denominator is (x² − 1)/x².
questions.hint: Rewrite the big fraction bar as ÷.

ex.main: **x/(x − 1).** Once it is a division, flip the bottom fraction and cancel. (x − 1)/x is the reciprocal of the answer — what you get by flipping the top instead — and (x + 1)²(x − 1)/x³ multiplies without flipping.
ex.tip: A complex fraction is just A ÷ B written vertically.

questions.q: Box A is a cube with edge 2x. Box B has a square base x by x and height 4x. The more efficient box has the smaller ratio of surface area to volume. Which is it?
opts: Neither: both boxes simplify to the same ratio, 3/x
Box B: its ratio is 9/(2x), which is less than 3/x
Box A: its ratio is 3/x, against 9/(2x) for Box B
It depends on x, so neither box is better at every size
questions.hint: Find SA and V for each box, then simplify SA/V.
steps: Box A: SA = 6(2x)² = 24x², V = (2x)³ = 8x³, so SA/V = 3/x.
Box B: SA = 2x² + 4(x · 4x) = 18x², V = 4x³, so SA/V = 9/(2x).
9/(2x) = 4.5/x, which is bigger than 3/x for every positive x.
Box A, the cube, is more efficient.

ex.main: **Box A.** Both ratios have the form (number)/x, so comparing the numbers 3 and 4.5 decides it once and for all — "it depends on x" is exactly what the simplification rules out. The cube wins, as compact shapes always do.
ex.tip: When two ratios share the same x-part, only the coefficients need comparing.

questions.q: A classmate simplifies (x² + 6x)/(x² + 3x) by crossing out the x² terms and gets 6x/3x = 2. What is the correct result?
questions.hint: Factor x out of the top and the bottom.
steps: Top: x² + 6x = x(x + 6). Bottom: x² + 3x = x(x + 3).
Both 0 and −3 made the original bottom zero, so x ≠ 0, −3.

ex.main: **(x + 6)/(x + 3), for x ≠ 0, −3.** The x² terms are terms, not factors, so they cannot be crossed out. A quick check: at x = 1 the original is 7/4, not 2. Dropping the restriction x ≠ 0 is the subtler error — the x cancelled, but x = 0 still breaks the original.
ex.tip: One numerical check would have caught the classmate's answer.

questions.q: Is (3x + 8)/(2x + 8) = 3/2 always, sometimes, or never true?
questions.hint: Solve the equation rather than cancelling the 8s.
steps: No value of x works, so it is never true.

ex.main: **Never.** "Cancelling the 8s" suggests always, but 8 is a term, not a factor. At x = 0 the left side is 8/8 = 1, and at x = 8 it is 32/24 = 4/3 — neither is 3/2, and the algebra shows no x ever will be.
ex.tip: A false statement like 16 = 24 at the end means no solution at all.

questions.q: How does the graph of f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) compare with the graph of g(x) = x + 3?
opts: They are identical at every single point
The same line, except f has a hole at (3, 6)
f has a vertical asymptote at x = 3, and g does not
The same line, except f has a hole at (−3, 0)
questions.hint: Simplify f, then ask which x it cannot accept.
steps: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so f simplifies to x + 3.
But f is undefined at x = 3, where its original denominator is 0.
The factor x − 3 cancelled, so x = 3 is a hole, not an asymptote.

ex.main: **The same line, except f has a hole at (3, 6).** The simplification is valid everywhere except x = 3, so the graphs agree at every other point. A cancelled factor gives a hole, never an asymptote, and (−3, 0) is just where the line crosses the x-axis.
ex.tip: This is why the domain has to travel with a simplified answer.

questions.q: Divide and simplify: (2x² − 7x − 4)/(x² − 9) ÷ (2x + 1)/(x + 3). State the domain.
questions.hint: Factor 2x² − 7x − 4, flip the divisor, and collect restrictions from all three places.
steps: Restrictions: x ≠ 3, −3 from x² − 9, and x ≠ −½ from the divisor's numerator.

ex.main: **(x − 4)/(x − 3), for x ≠ 3, −3, −½.** Two options have the right expression with too few restrictions: −3 comes from the original denominators, and −½ from the divisor's numerator 2x + 1. (x + 4) is a factoring sign error.
ex.tip: The answer and the domain are both part of "simplify".

questions.q: A rectangle has area (x² + 7x + 10)/(x − 1) square units and width (x + 2)/(x² − 1) units. What is its length?
questions.hint: Length = area ÷ width.

ex.main: **(x + 5)(x + 1).** Area ÷ width, with the width flipped. (x + 2)²(x + 5)/((x − 1)²(x + 1)) multiplies the area by the width instead of dividing; (x + 5)/(x + 1) flips the area instead of the width.
ex.tip: Check the units: square units ÷ units = units, which only division gives.
